title: Searching for Massive Remnant Planetary System Hosts with White Dwarf Gaia XP Spectra
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Remnant planetary systems around massive white dwarfs ($M_{\rm WD} > 0.8\,{\rm M}_\odot$) are intrinsically rare and remain poorly characterized. As the evolutionary endpoints of intermediate-mass B- and A-type stars, these white dwarfs provide valuable constraints on the formation and survival of planetary systems around higher-mass progenitors. In the absence of large, dedicated spectroscopic surveys, extremely-low-resolution Gaia XP spectra provide a powerful means of identifying candidate metal-polluted white dwarfs. We obtained follow-up observations with low-resolution optical spectroscopy (R=500-4000) to search primarily for Ca II H & K absorption in massive, metal-polluted white dwarf candidates selected from Gaia XP spectra to increase the sample of massive remnant planetary system hosts among objects with effective temperatures below $\sim15{,}000$ K. We find that Gaia XP spectra recover metal-polluted white dwarfs efficiently, confirming 82$\pm$5% recovery of photospheric metals (59 of 72 targets) in high-confidence candidates of our sample (with classifier probability $P_{\rm DZ} > 0.65$). However, Gaia photometric masses derived from $G$, $G_{BP}$, and $G_{RP}$ broad-band photometry are not sufficient to identify the most massive systems, as reliable mass determinations require detailed metal-enriched atmospheric fits. We present a selection of cool white dwarfs confirmed to be both massive and metal polluted, demonstrating that Gaia XP spectra can substantially expand the sample of white dwarf exoplanet hosts. Our search led to the discovery of a new transiting debris system, SDSS J1624+5404, the 21st published system to date and eighth to show periodic transits.

AI.tldr: Gaia XP spectra efficiently identify metal-polluted massive white dwarf candidates, but accurate mass determination requires detailed atmospheric fits. Follow-up spectroscopy confirmed 82% of high-confidence candidates, yielding new remnant planetary system hosts including a new transiting debris system.
AI.motivation: Remnant planetary systems around massive white dwarfs (M_WD > 0.8 M_sun) are intrinsically rare and poorly characterized. As endpoints of intermediate-mass B- and A-type stars, they constrain planet formation and survival around higher-mass progenitors, but large dedicated spectroscopic surveys are lacking.
AI.method: Used extremely-low-resolution Gaia XP spectra to select massive, metal-polluted white dwarf candidates (T_eff < ~15,000 K), then obtained follow-up low-resolution optical spectroscopy (R=500-4000), primarily searching for Ca II H & K absorption. Masses were assessed via Gaia broad-band photometry (G, G_BP, G_RP) and detailed metal-enriched atmospheric fits.
AI.result: Gaia XP spectra recover metal-polluted white dwarfs efficiently, with 82±5% recovery of photospheric metals (59 of 72 targets) in high-confidence candidates (P_DZ > 0.65). Gaia photometric masses are insufficient to identify the most massive systems. The search produced a selection of confirmed cool, massive, metal-polluted white dwarfs and discovered a new transiting debris system, SDSS J1624+5404.
AI.conclusion: Gaia XP spectra can substantially expand the sample of white dwarf exoplanet hosts. However, reliable mass determinations require detailed metal-enriched atmospheric fits rather than broad-band photometric masses. SDSS J1624+5404 is the 21st published such system and the 8th to show periodic transits.

title: Multi-Epoch Stability in the Rotational Modulation of the Planetary-Mass Companion Ross 458C
summary: Spectroscopic variability is detected in brown dwarfs across all spectral types, suggesting atmospheric patchiness in brown dwarf atmospheres. We present JWST/NIRSpec time series observations of the T8.0 planetary-mass companion Ross 458C. We compared our derived spectral variability and light curve to those obtained using HST/WFC3 observations more than 7.5 yr before and published by Manjavacas et al. (2019). We found that the light curve of Ross 458C is remarkably similar in the two epochs in terms of shape and variability amplitude potentially created by stable weather patterns. We measured a rotational period of 11.57+\-0.09 hr, demonstrating that the previously reported HST/WFC3 period of 6.75+\-1.58 hr is most likely a second-order harmonic produced by an unresolved double-peaked rotational modulation, likely due to the higher uncertainties of the HST/WFC3 light curve and the short time baseline of those observations. We measured the variability amplitude in the white light curve created using only the wavelength range covered by HST/WFC3 (1.10-1.63 micron), obtaining a value of 1.47+\-0.18%, which is consistent with that measured in the HST/WFC3 light curve.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec time series of the T8.0 companion Ross 458C reveal a stable, double-peaked rotational modulation with a period of 11.57 hr, revising the earlier HST/WFC3 period of 6.75 hr, which was likely a harmonic artifact.
AI.motivation: Spectroscopic variability is seen across all brown dwarf spectral types, pointing to atmospheric patchiness, yet the temporal stability of such weather patterns and the reliability of previously reported rotational periods (often from short-baseline HST/WFC3 data) remain uncertain.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec time series observations of the T8.0 planetary-mass companion Ross 458C were used to derive a spectral variability and light curve, which were compared with HST/WFC3 observations taken more than 7.5 yr earlier (Manjavacas et al. 2019). The rotational period was fit from the new light curve, and the variability amplitude was measured in a white light curve restricted to the HST/WFC3 wavelength range (1.10–1.63 micron) for a direct comparison.
AI.result: The two-epoch light curves of Ross 458C are remarkably similar in shape and variability amplitude, suggesting stable weather patterns. A rotational period of 11.57 +/- 0.09 hr was measured, indicating the earlier HST/WFC3 period of 6.75 +/- 1.58 hr is most likely a second-order harmonic from an unresolved double-peaked modulation. The white light variability amplitude of 1.47 +/- 0.18% matches the HST/WFC3 value.
AI.conclusion: Ross 458C exhibits persistent, likely double-peaked rotational modulation over multi-year baselines, and the JWST-derived 11.57 hr period supersedes the shorter HST/WFC3 period, whose ambiguity stemmed from higher uncertainties and a short time baseline.

title: Stellar ages from [C/N] in giant stars: applicability and limitations
comment: Paper accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The [C/N] abundance ratio is a powerful age indicator for giant stars, enabling age estimates for spectroscopic samples where traditional methods are limited. We calibrate a multivariate [C/N]-age-[Fe/H] relationship using 9,122 giant stars observed by Kepler, with asteroseismic ages and APOGEE DR17 abundances. The calibration is performed separately for lower red giant branch (LRGB), upper RGB (URGB), and red clump (RC) stars. We validate the relationships using independent samples from K2, TESS, and open clusters, finding good agreement with reference ages, particularly for LRGB stars, with typical precision of ~30% for ages between ~2 - 10 Gyr. The performance degrades for URGB and RC stars and low metallicities, likely due to extra mixing processes, for young (<2 Gyr) and old (>10 Gyr) stars, where the [C/N]-age correlation weakens. We show that the [C/N]-based ages reproduce known Milky Way features, including the age distribution across the [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] plane and the flaring of the Galactic disc. Compared to other chemical clocks, [C/N] provides more robust and precise age estimates within its domain of validity. Our results demonstrate that [C/N], combined with metallicity, is an effective empirical tool for deriving stellar ages of giant stars from spectroscopic surveys, particularly for LRGB stars with [Fe/H] > -1, enabling Galactic archaeology studies beyond the reach of current asteroseismic samples.

AI.tldr: The paper calibrates a multivariate [C/N]-age-[Fe/H] relation using 9,122 Kepler giant stars with asteroseismic ages and APOGEE DR17 abundances, validated across K2, TESS, and open clusters, to derive ages for large spectroscopic samples.
AI.motivation: Asteroseismic ages are limited to relatively small samples, while spectroscopic surveys cover vastly more stars. The [C/N] abundance ratio serves as a powerful age indicator for giant stars, offering a way to estimate ages for spectroscopic samples where traditional methods cannot be applied, thus extending Galactic archaeology beyond current asteroseismic reach.
AI.method: The authors calibrate a multivariate [C/N]-age-[Fe/H] relationship using 9,122 giant stars from Kepler, combining asteroseismic ages with APOGEE DR17 abundances. Calibrations are performed separately for lower red giant branch (LRGB), upper RGB (URGB), and red clump (RC) stars. Validation uses independent samples from K2, TESS, and open clusters, and the derived ages are compared against other chemical clocks and used to reproduce known Milky Way features.
AI.result: The calibrated relations agree well with reference ages, especially for LRGB stars, achieving typical precision of ~30% for ages between ~2-10 Gyr. Performance degrades for URGB and RC stars, at low metallicities (likely due to extra mixing), and for very young (<2 Gyr) or very old (>10 Gyr) stars where the [C/N]-age correlation weakens. The [C/N]-based ages reproduce known Milky Way features, including the age distribution in the [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] plane and Galactic disc flaring. Compared to other chemical clocks, [C/N] yields more robust and precise ages within its validity domain.
AI.conclusion: [C/N], combined with metallicity, is an effective empirical tool for deriving stellar ages of giant stars from spectroscopic surveys, particularly for LRGB stars with [Fe/H] > -1. It enables Galactic archaeology studies beyond the reach of current asteroseismic samples.

title: Stellar Yields of Rapidly Rotating Population III Stars for the High Redshift Universe
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome
summary: JWST has revealed rapid nitrogen enrichment in high redshift galaxies, renewing the need for stellar yields that follow metal free stars beyond the main sequence and across their final fates. We present Geneva stellar evolution models of rapidly rotating Pop~III stars with $5 \leq M_{\rm ini}/M_\odot \leq 200$ and $\upsilon_{\rm ini}/\upsilon_{\rm crit}=0.7$, evolved to the end of core O-burning. We calculate gross adopted ejecta masses using fate dependent remnant prescriptions spanning core collapse, pulsational pair instability, and complete pair instability. Our quantitative results focus on hydrostatically produced CNO material, while heavier species are treated as final-model reservoirs. Rotation produces primary CNO material by mixing newly synthesized C and O into H-burning layers, where CNO cycling generates nitrogen. The resulting abundance signature depends strongly on which stellar layers escape. Models leaving compact remnants can reach $\log({\rm N/O})=-0.49$ while remaining poor in Si/S/Ar/Ca-rich material. PISN models eject the largest nitrogen masses, $M_{\rm N}=1.8$--$2.5,M_\odot$, but also release $57$--$65,M_\odot$ of oxygen, lowering $\log({\rm N/O})$ to $-1.44$ to $-1.29$. Thus, high nitrogen yields do not imply high N/O ratios. This trend persists after IMF weighting, as increasingly top-heavy populations add oxygen and deep alpha material faster than they build a nitrogen dominated mixture. Our grid provides a new CNO-focused prompt-enrichment dataset for interpreting nitrogen-rich systems including GN-z11, CEERS-1019, and GS~3073.

AI.tldr: Rotating metal-free (Pop III) Geneva models from 5–200 M☉ evolved to core O-burning show that rotation-driven primary CNO production yields high nitrogen masses but low N/O ratios, since PISN ejecta co-release large oxygen masses.
AI.motivation: JWST observations reveal rapid nitrogen enrichment in high-redshift galaxies, creating a need for stellar yield models of metal-free stars that extend beyond the main sequence through their final evolutionary fates.
AI.method: Geneva stellar evolution models of rapidly rotating Pop III stars (5 ≤ M_ini/M☉ ≤ 200, υ_ini/υ_crit = 0.7) evolved to the end of core O-burning. Gross ejecta masses computed via fate-dependent remnant prescriptions covering core collapse, pulsational pair instability, and complete pair instability. Analysis focuses on hydrostatically produced CNO material, with heavier species treated as final-model reservoirs.
AI.result: Rotation mixes newly synthesized C and O into H-burning layers, where CNO cycling makes nitrogen. Abundance signatures depend strongly on escaping layers. Compact-remnant models reach log(N/O) = −0.49 while poor in Si/S/Ar/Ca-rich material. PISN models eject the largest nitrogen masses (M_N = 1.8–2.5 M☉) but also release 57–65 M☉ of oxygen, lowering log(N/O) to −1.44 to −1.29. IMF weighting preserves the trend as top-heavy populations add oxygen and deep alpha material faster than nitrogen.
AI.conclusion: High nitrogen yields do not imply high N/O ratios. The grid provides a new CNO-focused prompt-enrichment dataset for interpreting nitrogen-rich systems such as GN-z11, CEERS-1019, and GS 3073.

title: The JWST Ultramassive Galaxy Sample -- I. Overview, Photometry, and Stellar Kinematics: Selecting Optimal Template Subsets via Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, LaTeX. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We introduce the JWST Ultramassive Galaxy Sample, comprising 8 extreme early-type galaxies ($M_\star \gtrsim 2\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) drawn as a representative subset from a comprehensive full-sky census of over 100 such objects. This program aims to dynamically measure their central supermassive black holes (BHs) to probe the extreme high-mass end of BH--galaxy scaling relations, a critical regime where the physical mechanisms governing BH growth and host-galaxy co-evolution are expected to fundamentally change. In this first paper, we present the foundational data products: detailed photometric models and spatially resolved nuclear stellar kinematics. To accurately map the stellar mass distribution from the BH sphere of influence out to the extended halo, we combine diffraction-limited JWST/NIRCam imaging with wide-field DESI Legacy Surveys data, parametrizing the surface brightness using Multi-Gaussian Expansion (MGE). We extract stellar kinematics from JWST/NIRSpec integral-field observations using the penalized pixel-fitting (\textsc{pPXF}) method. To fully exploit the continuous $1.66-3.17\,μ\mathrm{m}$ wavelength coverage---avoiding the telluric gaps of ground-based empirical libraries and the computational burden of massive theoretical grids---we introduce the use of near-separable Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). This algorithm identifies an optimal, highly compressed subset of synthetic spectra from the updated BOSZ library, perfectly capturing its spanning power at a fraction of the computational cost. The resulting kinematic maps reveal that these ultramassive systems are overwhelmingly slow rotators, frequently harboring kinematically decoupled cores. These high-quality photometric and kinematic data provide the inputs required for the robust Jeans Anisotropic Modelling (JAM) of the central BH masses in Paper II.

AI.tldr: Introduces the JWST Ultramassive Galaxy Sample (8 extreme early-type galaxies, M⋆ ≳ 2×10^12 M⊙) and presents foundational photometric models and spatially resolved nuclear stellar kinematics from JWST NIRCam/NIRSpec, using MGE modeling and a novel near-separable NMF approach for kinematic fitting.
AI.motivation: To dynamically measure central supermassive black holes in ultramassive galaxies and probe the extreme high-mass end of BH–galaxy scaling relations, a regime where BH growth and host-galaxy co-evolution mechanisms are expected to fundamentally change.
AI.method: Combines diffraction-limited JWST/NIRCam imaging with wide-field DESI Legacy Surveys data, parametrizing surface brightness via Multi-Gaussian Expansion (MGE) to map stellar mass from the BH sphere of influence to the extended halo. Stellar kinematics are extracted from JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations using pPXF, with near-separable Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) applied to a compressed subset of synthetic spectra from the updated BOSZ library over continuous 1.66–3.17 μm coverage.
AI.result: The NMF approach captures the library's spanning power at a fraction of the computational cost, avoiding telluric gaps of ground-based libraries and the burden of massive theoretical grids. Kinematic maps show these ultramassive systems are overwhelmingly slow rotators, frequently harboring kinematically decoupled cores.
AI.conclusion: The photometric and kinematic data provide the inputs required for robust Jeans Anisotropic Modelling (JAM) of central BH masses in Paper II.

title: The JWST Ultramassive Galaxy Sample -- II. Supermassive Black Hole Masses for 8 Extreme Early-Type Galaxies via Jeans Anisotropic Modelling of High-Resolution Integral-Field NIRSpec Stellar Kinematics
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, LaTeX. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present central supermassive black hole (BH) mass measurements for the JWST Ultramassive Galaxy Sample, comprising 8 galaxies selected from a complete sample of the most massive early-type galaxies in the nearby Universe ($M_\star \gtrsim 2\times10^{12} M_\odot$). Building on the MGE photometric profiles and JWST/NIRSpec stellar kinematics from Paper I, we use the Jeans Anisotropic Modelling (JAM) framework to reconstruct the nuclear dynamics. Given the unique structural properties of these dry-merger-dominated systems, our Bayesian MCMC analysis explicitly tests both oblate and prolate intrinsic geometries. By marginalizing over classical dynamical degeneracies (including orbital velocity anisotropy, mass-to-light ratios, and inclination), we extract robust BH masses. We demonstrate that JWST's exceptional resolution allows JAM to tightly constrain the central potential using nuclear kinematics alone. Crucially, not all ultramassive galaxies host ultramassive BHs: while most display a classic central velocity dispersion peak, notable exceptions emerge, including a clear central dispersion drop in one galaxy and a subdued peak in another. These kinematic differences yield distinct BH masses, suggesting BH growth at extreme mass scales is highly stochastic. This stochasticity may be driven by three-body ejections during hierarchical mergers or gravitational recoil kicks from coalescing binaries. In the latter case, the kicked BH may be displaced and wandering outside the compact NIRSpec field of view. Our derived BH masses populate the historically sparse upper envelope of the galaxy mass hierarchy, providing the critical foundation for Paper III to investigate extreme-mass BH scaling relations and test models of galaxy-BH co-evolution.

AI.tldr: JWST Ultramassive Galaxy Sample (8 nearby early-type galaxies) yields central SMBH masses via JAM modeling, revealing widely varying BH masses and stochastic BH growth at extreme mass scales.
AI.motivation: The most massive early-type galaxies host sparsely measured central black holes; understanding BH growth and galaxy-BH co-evolution at extreme mass scales requires robust mass measurements in these systems.
AI.method: Using MGE photometric profiles and JWST/NIRSpec stellar kinematics (Paper I), the authors apply Jeans Anisotropic Modelling (JAM) with Bayesian MCMC, testing both oblate and prolate geometries and marginalizing over anisotropy, mass-to-light ratio, and inclination.
AI.result: JWST resolution tightly constrains the central potential from nuclear kinematics. Not all ultramassive galaxies host ultramassive BHs—most show central velocity dispersion peaks, but one has a clear central dispersion drop and another a subdued peak, yielding distinct BH masses and suggesting highly stochastic BH growth.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic BH growth at extreme scales may arise from three-body ejections in hierarchical mergers or gravitational recoil kicks (possibly displacing the BH outside the NIRSpec field of view). The derived masses populate the sparse upper envelope of the galaxy mass hierarchy, forming the basis for Paper III on extreme-mass BH scaling relations.

title: Stochastic black hole growth tracks stellar mass in ultramassive galaxies
summary: Over the past three decades, it has been established that galaxy spheroids contain supermassive black holes (BHs) whose masses correlate tightly with the properties of their host galaxies. The most predictive of these correlations is between BH mass and stellar velocity dispersion (the $M_{\rm BH}-σ$ relation), alongside a relation with bulge luminosity or stellar mass (the $M_{\rm BH}-M_\star$ relation). Theoretical models of galaxy evolution predict that for the most massive galaxies, whose late-time growth proceeds mainly via gas-poor `dry' mergers, $M_\star$ should become a better predictor of BH mass than $σ$. However, genuine deviations from the $M_{\rm BH}-σ$ relation have remained difficult to observe due to the extreme rarity and low central surface brightness of such galaxies. Here we report James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) measurements of central BHs in a sample of eight ultramassive galaxies. We find the largest deviations from the $M_{\rm BH}-σ$ relation ever reported, with most BH masses exceeding $10^{10}$ solar masses. In this extreme mass regime, the galaxies tightly follow the $M_{\rm BH}-M_\star$ relation with minimal scatter, successfully confirming theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we observe significant stochasticity: For one ultramassive galaxy, the central dispersion drops rather than peaks, revealing no evidence for a central mass; while we can formally only place an upper limit, the data are entirely consistent with no BH at all. Crucially, this physical dichotomy is already evident directly in the raw kinematic maps prior to any fitting, and is robustly confirmed by our dynamical modelling. This unexpected diversity suggests that extreme multi-body dynamical processes, such as gravitational recoil or three-body ejections, significantly disrupt BH growth in the Universe's most massive galaxies.

AI.tldr: JWST measures central black holes in eight ultramassive galaxies, finding the largest deviations from the M_BH-σ relation ever reported, while the galaxies tightly follow the M_BH-M_star relation with minimal scatter, confirming theoretical predictions. One galaxy shows no evidence for a central black hole, suggesting extreme dynamical processes disrupt black hole growth.
AI.motivation: For three decades, galaxy spheroids have been known to host supermassive black holes whose masses correlate with host galaxy properties, most predictively via the M_BH-σ relation. Theoretical models predict that for the most massive galaxies, which grow mainly via gas-poor 'dry' mergers, stellar mass (M_star) should become a better predictor of BH mass than velocity dispersion (σ). However, genuine deviations from the M_BH-σ relation have been hard to observe due to the extreme rarity and low central surface brightness of such galaxies.
AI.method: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) measurements of central black holes in a sample of eight ultramassive galaxies, using raw kinematic maps and dynamical modelling.
AI.result: The authors find the largest deviations from the M_BH-σ relation ever reported, with most BH masses exceeding 10^10 solar masses. In this extreme mass regime, the galaxies tightly follow the M_BH-M_star relation with minimal scatter, confirming theoretical predictions. They also observe significant stochasticity: for one ultramassive galaxy, the central dispersion drops rather than peaks, revealing no evidence for a central mass; while only an upper limit can be formally placed, the data are entirely consistent with no BH at all. This physical dichotomy is evident directly in the raw kinematic maps prior to fitting and is confirmed by dynamical modelling.
AI.conclusion: The unexpected diversity suggests that extreme multi-body dynamical processes, such as gravitational recoil or three-body ejections, significantly disrupt black hole growth in the Universe's most massive galaxies.

authors: Clara E. Martínez-Vásquez Clecio R. Bom
title: Discovery, Characterization, and Potential Origins of a Stream in the Stellar Halo of Nearby LMC-Mass Galaxy NGC 55
summary: We present a previously undetected stellar stream in the halo of the LMC-mass dwarf galaxy NGC 55 (2 Mpc), as part of an ongoing effort to characterize the stellar halos of LMC/SMC-mass dwarfs in the DEEP component of the DECam Local Volume Exploration (DELVE) survey. This structure is aligned with an outflow traced by H$α$ emission, a spur and cloud of neutral hydrogen, and the ultra-diffuse and possibly disrupting satellite galaxy NGC 55-dw1. We investigate possible ex-situ progenitor scenarios for this stream through the local luminosity-metallicity relation and a set of toy dynamical models that include gaseous, stellar, and dark matter components. If the stream is a product of a previous merger, the progenitor galaxy had an absolute magnitude $M_V \leq -7.2$ and a stellar mass $M_* \geq 10^5 M_{\odot}$ based on extrapolations of the detected stellar populations. If it is disrupted material from the ultra-diffuse satellite, their shared progenitor had an absolute magnitude $M_V \leq -8.3$ and a stellar mass $M_* \geq 10^{5.2} M_{\odot}$. We compare our stream and progenitor scenarios to those for NGC 300, a galaxy with a stellar mass similar to that of NGC~55 and known to host multiple structures in its halo. Our results demonstrate that even relatively isolated LMC-mass galaxies can have complex accretion histories, providing new tests of hierarchical galaxy formation at low masses.

AI.tldr: A previously undetected stellar stream is found in the halo of the LMC-mass dwarf NGC 55, aligned with an outflow, HI features, and the ultra-diffuse satellite NGC 55-dw1, suggesting a complex ex-situ accretion history.
AI.motivation: To characterize the stellar halos of LMC/SMC-mass dwarfs within the DEEP component of the DELVE survey, testing hierarchical galaxy formation at low masses, since even relatively isolated LMC-mass galaxies may have complex accretion histories.
AI.method: The stream is identified in NGC 55 (2 Mpc) halo imaging. Ex-situ progenitor scenarios are tested using the local luminosity-metallicity relation and toy dynamical models incorporating gaseous, stellar, and dark matter components; progenitor properties are inferred from extrapolations of detected stellar populations, with comparison to NGC 300.
AI.result: The stream aligns with an H-alpha outflow, a spur and cloud of neutral hydrogen, and the ultra-diffuse, possibly disrupting satellite NGC 55-dw1. For a merger origin, the progenitor had M_V <= -7.2 and M_* >= 10^5 M_sun; for disrupted material from the ultra-diffuse satellite, the shared progenitor had M_V <= -8.3 and M_* >= 10^5.2 M_sun.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate that relatively isolated LMC-mass galaxies can host complex accretion histories, offering new tests of hierarchical galaxy formation at low masses and motivating comparison with systems like NGC 300.

title: The AGN Channel in 3D: Scattering Belts and the Importance of Eccentricity in the Black Hole Population
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are a promising origin for observed gravitational wave mergers. Current population synthesis models are limited to 1D N-body or Monte Carlo methods which rely on statistical approaches to resolving dynamical scatterings. We present three-dimensional hybrid $N$-body simulations of a population of black holes (BHs) surrounding an AGN using a new code in development, AGNBI, where close interactions are directly simulated for both single and binary objects. Our results show binary formations occur throughout the AGN disk, particularly where the migration time is long. While BHs efficiently migrate and pair up in migration traps, they are frequently disrupted by ionisation or exchanges from binary-single and binary-binary interactions. We report a broadened radial distribution of formations and mergers about the trap radius when accounting for binary-single and binary-binary interactions, which we describe as a "scattering belt''. We assess the influence of the pre-existing BH population. When we model a non-zero eccentricity distribution in the BH population, the binary formations and mergers are suppressed by an order of magnitude compared to a non-eccentric population as fewer BHs embed in the AGN disk. We report an approximate merger rate of $\mathcal{R}_\mathrm{GW}\approx2\text{--}12\,\mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ with maximum BH masses of $10^2\text{--}10^3\,M_\odot$ through hierarchical mergers, where lower initial velocity dispersions produce larger BHs. The mass and mass ratio distributions are comparatively flat, suggesting AGN may be more relevant for high-mass or unequal-mass gravitational wave sources.

AI.tldr: 3D hybrid N-body simulations with the AGNBI code show that black holes in AGN disks form binaries broadly across the disk via a "scattering belt," with mergers and hierarchical growth producing GW events at ~2–12 Gpc⁻³ yr⁻¹.
AI.motivation: AGN are a promising channel for gravitational wave mergers, but existing population synthesis models are limited to 1D N-body or Monte Carlo methods that resolve dynamical scatterings only statistically, missing detailed close-interaction dynamics.
AI.method: The authors perform three-dimensional hybrid N-body simulations of a BH population around an AGN using the new code AGNBI, directly simulating close interactions for single and binary objects, including binary-single and binary-binary interactions, pre-existing BH populations, and eccentricity distributions.
AI.result: Binary formation occurs throughout the AGN disk, especially where migration time is long; BHs migrate and pair in migration traps but are frequently disrupted by ionization or exchanges. Binary-single and binary-binary interactions broaden the radial distribution of formations and mergers around the trap radius into a "scattering belt." A non-zero eccentricity BH distribution suppresses formations and mergers by an order of magnitude. Mergers occur at R_GW ≈ 2–12 Gpc⁻³ yr⁻¹, with maximum BH masses of 10²–10³ M☉ via hierarchical mergers, where lower initial velocity dispersions yield larger BHs.
AI.conclusion: The comparatively flat mass and mass ratio distributions suggest AGN disks may be more relevant for high-mass or unequal-mass gravitational wave sources.
